paras: The killing of Fletcher Reeves was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Patrolman R. L. Leath at a Black dance pavilion in Gadsden, Alabama, at midnight on the night of August 11-12, 1910. Leath was arresting Reeves for selling whiskey, and the only published account, a brief dispatch carrying the officer's version, said Reeves struck him and tried to take his gun. The dispatch ran in white papers in at least three states within a week, and no Black-press coverage was found.

According to the Gadsden dispatch, Reeves had come to the city from Chattanooga "with a large supply of liquor and was selling it." The papers described him only as "a negro whiskey seller" and gave no age, occupation or family.

Around midnight Reeves was selling whiskey at what the dispatch called "a negro dance pavilion" when Leath placed him under arrest. In the officer's account as printed, Reeves then struck Leath and "attempted to take his gun from him." Leath shot him through the heart, and Reeves died instantly. No account from Reeves's side, from people at the dance, or from other witnesses appears in the coverage.
No report of an inquest, a grand jury inquiry or any charge against Leath was found in the coverage.

The story reached readers as a single short dispatch datelined Gadsden, August 12. On August 13 the Montgomery Advertiser printed it without a headline among Alabama briefs, while the Pensacola Journal ran it on its front page under the heading "PAROLMAN KILLS NEGRO." Five days later the Johnson City Comet headlined it "NEGRO WHISKY SELLER SHOT BY PATROLMAN," and the Bamberg Herald in South Carolina ran it as "Patrolman Slays Negro," naming the victim only as "F. Reeves."

Each version repeated the officer's explanation as plain fact, without attribution, and identified Reeves throughout as "the negro." The case also surfaced, unnamed, in a Newberry, South Carolina, column in which "The Idler" listed "A patrolman in Alabama slays a negro" among the crime stories in one issue of the Columbia Record, as an example of reading he found unhelpful rather than as a matter of concern in itself. No coverage of the killing was found in the Black press.

accounts.label: Wire report (officer's version)
accounts.gist: Reeves was selling whiskey at a Black dance pavilion; when Leath arrested him he struck the officer and tried to take his gun, and Leath shot him through the heart, killing him instantly.

framing.detail: Papers in Florida, Alabama, Tennessee and South Carolina ran the same dispatch under headlines such as 'PAROLMAN KILLS NEGRO' and 'NEGRO WHISKY SELLER SHOT BY PATROLMAN', with the officer's account unattributed.
A Newberry columnist cited 'A patrolman in Alabama slays a negro' as one item in a list of crime stories he thought papers printed too much of.

conflicts.note: Abbreviation in one reprint, not a real disagreement; the Pensacola OCR reads 'Reevea'.

record_check.dossier: Midnight on the night of Aug. 11-12, 1910; the Aug. 12 dispatch says 'midnight last night', so the shooting may fall on Aug. 11 by calendar date
Shot in the course of an arrest at the pavilion, not while held in jail; context is arrest
